transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Devon Cole (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Orchid HT), Maya Chen (Orchid Infra), Sanjay Patel (Orchid CTO), Rina Alvarez (Orchid SRE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to validate kernel fallback behavior across TRT-LLM and vLLM on NVLink multi-GPU nodes; focus on persistent KV cache effects, CUDA graph stability during dynamic batching, and NUMA/eviction prefetch interactions for long-context inference. Agreed next steps to exchange logs and run a short on-prem pilot.

Topics covered:
- Kernel selection heuristics and fallback transitions
- CUDA Graph instantiation vs dynamic replay
- Persistent KV cache eviction/prefetch behavior across GPUs/NVLink
- Quantization tradeoffs for TRT-LLM vs vLLM exec paths
- Observability: per-token latency traces, kernel histograms, and perf counters
- Security/ops: VPC, KMS, SOC2 artifacts for private deployment

Action items (recap included above).

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): All right, hey everyone, thanks for carving time. We got about an hour and change. I'll hand to Priya to kick off with the profiler recap.
[00:00:15] Priya (Redwood SE): Cool, thanks. So, quick context — we ran two microbenchmarks on your NVLink 4-GPU nodes, one with TRT-LLM optimized kernels and one with vLLM path, and we saw two interesting things: first, kernel switching during long contexts with mixed batch sizes, and second, intermittent CUDA graph instantiation stalls when the persistent KV cache is large.
[00:00:45] Maya (Customer): Sorry, can you define "kernel switching" in this context? Like, you mean the runtime chooses a different GEMM kernel mid-sequence?
[00:00:52] Priya: Yeah, exactly. The runtime selects kernel variants based on sequence length and memory layout; in TRT-LLM the compiled paths are more static but we do have a fallback to a more generic kernel when some assumptions break — for example, when KV cache page faults or when cuBLAS heuristic picks a different algo. vLLM often uses JIT faster paths but then hits different aten/cuda kernels.
[00:01:18] Liam: And does that fallback cause latency spikes? We saw some 100-300ms jumps on tails during our long-doc tests.
[00:01:26] Priya: Yes, we repro'd spikes. Typically it's the first token after a fallback or after a CUDA graph replay boundary. There's a small stall while kernels rebind and the KV cache pointers are reconciled across GPUs.
[00:01:41] Devon (Redwood SE): To add: NVLink adds another surface — when KV pages are evicted locally and fetched over NVLink you see a tail that aligns with NRQ stalls. We instrumented PCIe vs NVLink traces and the pattern matched the latency tail.
[00:02:00] Sanjay (Customer): NRQ stalls? Sorry, that's a new acronym for us.
[00:02:03] Devon: My bad, I meant NVRAM read queue analogy — not a standard term, sorry — point is the link saturation and remote page fetches cause the spike.
[00:02:12] Rina (SRE): We saw similar behavior last month when some jobs started rebalancing across GPUs. Do you think it's eviction policy? We run aggressive caching to save mem.
[00:02:21] Priya: Yes eviction policy is central. If persistent KV cache is too big relative to contiguous local memory, the runtime will evict, then prefetch on demand — that prefetch across NVLink costs time and sometimes triggers a fallback path that uses a slower kernel because the scheduler can't assume contiguous KV in L2.
[00:02:38] Liam: Would quantization change that? If we move to 4-bit TRT kernels we reduce KV size, maybe fewer evictions?
[00:02:45] Priya: In practice quantization helps but adds complexity. TRT-LLM 4-bit kernels reduce memory but require different kernel code paths; sometimes the reduced memory reduces evictions enough to stay on the fast path, but other times the quantized kernel itself is slightly slower per-op for some matrix shapes — so overall latency can be better or worse depending on distribution. We did an A/B across short-chat vs long-doc and saw long-doc tended to win with int4 on TRT, short-chat slightly favored vLLM float16.
[00:03:06] Liam: Hmm okay.
[00:03:09] Jordan: One thing we wanted to emphasize — batching strategy matters. Continuous batching with prefix caching avoids redundant KV fetches but if you allow dynamic batch sizes to change the trace the CUDA Graph will need to be re-recorded, which causes a brief instantiation cost.
[00:03:23] Maya: So is the recommendation to avoid dynamic batch shapes when using CUDA graphs?
[00:03:27] Priya: Either that or you pre-compile a set of graphs for common shape families and do fast graph switching. But switching graphs is still cheaper than falling back to a generic kernel in many cases. However, on NVLink multi-GPU nodes the graph switching must coordinate KV pointers across devices; if the pointers aren't pinned it's more brittle.
[00:03:44] Liam: Can you walk through an annotated trace? We looked at the perf logs you sent and got lost around the 00:27 mark.
[00:03:50] Priya: Sure — I have a snippet. (screen share) At 00:26:12 you see a pattern: sustained fast tokens at ~12ms, then a single 250ms spike. The trace shows a graph switch event immediately before the spike, followed by a fallback to a generic aten kernel. The root cause was an allocation failure when the runtime tried to pin the KV range for the new graph.
[00:04:20] Liam: Allocation failure as in out-of-memory? But we had free memory...
[00:04:24] Devon: It's subtle; fragmentation and NUMA affinity. On your nodes the jobs are pinned across NUMA domains, and the allocator couldn't find a contiguous block on GPU0, so it spilled to a fallback on GPU1 and the runtime triggered a kernel path change.
[00:04:39] Maya: That lines up with our ops logs — occasionally we see memory include fragmentation after multiple restarts. Any suggestions to avoid it?
[00:04:46] Priya: A few operational levers: 1) pre-warm allocator via a warmup step so contiguous blocks are carved; 2) set explicit NUMA/GPU pinning in workload orchestration; 3) reduce KV cache per shard or use shard-aware placement if you can. We'll share a short script to pre-allocate.
[00:05:03] Sanjay: Is that script safe for our production nodes? We can't risk affecting latency for other tenants.
[00:05:08] Jordan: Good call — for Dedicated or Private customers we recommend scheduling pre-warm on maintenance windows. For Hosted we handle that for you. On private installs you control scheduling.
[00:05:17] Rina: Security question — if KV is sharded across GPUs, is any data crossing NVLink unencrypted? We need to map to our KMS requirements.
[00:05:25] Priya: NVLink traffic itself isn't encrypted; Redwood supports TLS and we can integrate with HSM/KMS for key management of persisted artifacts. But cross-GPU traffic lives in memory; encryption at rest and access controls protect persisted KV. For regulated data you should run Private with our KMS integration.
[00:05:43] Maya: Does the on-prem package include kernel-level hooks or is it user-space only?
[00:05:48] Devon: It's user-space. We don't ship kernel modules. We rely on standard CUDA drivers. We provide hooks and a daemon to instrument and log kernel selections and graph events.
[00:05:58] Liam: Back to profiler: on the TRT side you mentioned sometimes compiled TRT engines choose slower algo on certain shapes. Can you elaborate?
[00:06:05] Priya: It's often about workspace size heuristics and cuBLAS/cuDNN choosing algo based on internal heuristics. TRT engine builder sometimes picks a kernel that's optimal for median shapes but not for the tail shapes in your workload. We recommend a tuning pass with representative requests. That generates a tuned engine set and minimizes fallback risk.
[00:06:26] Sanjay: How heavy is that tuning pass? Does it require GPU-hours?
[00:06:30] Priya: It depends on the diversity of shapes. For our customers it's often a few hours on a test cluster. We can run it as part of the pilot.
[00:06:36] Maya: You mentioned graph eviction instability earlier. What causes the graph to become invalidated?
[00:06:40] Devon: Two main causes: change in batch shape (requires re-record) and underlying allocator moving pinned pages. If the runtime unmaps and remaps memory regions the CUDA graph handle references invalid memory and the runtime must rebuild. Also driver-level preemption can invalidate assumptions.
[00:06:58] Liam: Could we mitigate by pinning GPU memory with cudaHostRegister or similar?
[00:07:02] Priya: Yes, pinning helps, but must be balanced with system-level constraints. Some clouds restrict pinned memory quotas.
[00:07:10] Jordan: Quick interjection — we tried a hybrid approach for another customer: keep a small hot-KV in pinned memory for fast-path tokens and shadow the rest in a quantized cold store. That reduced visible spikes by ~60% in our tests.
[00:07:24] Maya: What's shadowing mean operationally? Are you streaming the cold store over NVMe or remote node?
[00:07:29] Devon: Typically NVMe local to the node or a remote store, accessed via async prefetch. The key is to prefetch predicted keys before they're needed. It's workload dependent.
[00:07:38] Liam: Prediction sounds risky. How do you predict reliably for long-doc generation?
[00:07:43] Priya: Not perfect, but for multi-turn chat we can leverage prefix heuristics and beam sampling to guess the next token ranges. For document slicing we prefetch next segments based on sliding-window heuristics. We'll share the experimental heuristics script.
[00:07:57] Sanjay: Okay. Let's talk about observability — if we want per-token attribution to kernel, what do we need to instrument?
[00:08:03] Priya: Our SDK emits per-token events with kernel id, graph id, and wall time. On your side collect the GPU perf counters (SM utilization, L2 throughput) and nvprof traces for problem repro. We also recommend enabling our micro-trace which adds ~1% overhead but gives you kernel histograms.
[00:08:20] Liam: We have a question — when CUDA graph fails and you fall back, are you losing correctness or just performance?
[00:08:25] Devon: Mostly performance, not correctness. The fallback kernels are numerically equivalent to compiled kernels. Edge cases exist when mixed precision rounding changes slightly, but in practice outputs match within tolerance.
[00:08:38] Maya: Any specific driver versions we should lock to? We've got a mixed fleet.
[00:08:42] Priya: We recommend Nvidia driver NNN.1 or later with CUDA 12.x for TRT-LLM stability; for vLLM float16 paths CUDA 11.8+ is okay but we prefer 12.x for best kernel coverage. We'll send exact matrix.
[00:08:55] Liam: Can Redwood run the tuning pass inside our VPC so we don't send artifacts out?
[00:08:59] Jordan: Yes, for Private deployments we can run everything inside your VPC and we support node-level tooling for in-place profiling.
[00:09:06] Sanjay: Are there any licensing constraints with TRT engines for on-prem?
[00:09:10] Jordan: TRT is covered by NVIDIA licensing; Redwood's tooling generates and manages engines but your org controls the binary artifacts. We'll share the legal note.
[00:09:18] Maya: Let's go through a short repro scenario — we want to see a long-doc generation where kernels fall back at token ~1200. What do you need from us?
[00:09:26] Priya: Provide a 4-5MB document, model (we suggest Llama-70b-8k or equivalent), and your current batching config. We'll produce a runbook to reproduce with our profiler flags enabled.
[00:09:36] Liam: We'll get that to you.
[00:09:39] Jordan: Quick note on costs — TRT quantized engines reduce GPU memory and theoretical cost-per-token but may increase CPU preprocessing and engine build costs. We'll include an estimated delta in the spreadsheet.
[00:09:51] Rina: Anything we can do to minimize risk during the pilot?
[00:09:54] Priya: Run pilot on non-critical nodes, pin tenants, and schedule pre-warm. We'll provide a safe runbook.
[00:09:59] Devon: Also consider initial traffic shaping to avoid large fan-outs that saturate NVLink during prefetch.
[00:10:06] Sanjay: One more operational question: if we want to enable KMS/HSM for persisted KV blobs, how does that affect runtime?
[00:10:12] Priya: Minimal latency impact on read/write if you use envelope encryption — the per-token path reads decrypted in-memory. The main cost is on write/rotate and initial key unwrap which is async. We'll share integration guide.
[00:10:24] Jordan: Okay, we're at the meat of the call — Priya and Devon, can you run through the specific repro steps and point to the log entries now?
[00:10:31] Priya: (screen share) Step 1: run warmup with pinned allocations. Step 2: run inference with mixed batch sizes including singletons and batched requests to force graph switching. Step 3: trigger a KV growth event by sending a long-doc request at token 800. The logs in our sheet show graph switch markers and kernel id changes at those times. Look for log tag graph_rebuild and kernel_fallback.
[00:11:05] Liam: We see graph_rebuild entries, but kernel_fallback is sparse.
[00:11:09] Devon: You might be sampling at coarse granularity — increase trace resolution to 5ms buckets.
[00:11:15] Maya: Any chance these graph rebuilds are triggered by orchestration events (container restart, oom kill)? We saw a kube eviction around same time.
[00:11:22] Priya: Yes orchestration restarts will definitely cause rebuilds. We cross-referenced kube events and in some runs the graph rebuild follows a container restart by 200ms. Try to run an isolated container for repro.
[00:11:33] Sanjay: Are there things on our side to change in Kubernetes to reduce noise?
[00:11:36] Devon: Reserve GPU memory, avoid preemption, set QoS to guaranteed for pilot pods.
[00:11:42] Liam: Great. A slightly different topic — how does TRTexec engine warmup interact with runtime caching?
[00:11:47] Priya: Engine warmup pre-populates internal workspaces. It reduces first-token latency but doesn't change KV eviction mechanics. If you warmup with representative sequences you avoid many of the first-fallbacks.
[00:11:58] Maya: Can Redwood automate warmup during deployment?
[00:12:02] Jordan: Yes, our deploy flow includes optional warmup hooks. For Private deploys we give you the hook scripts.
[00:12:07] Liam: Okay, let's capture the final checklist so we leave with clear next steps.
[00:12:11] Jordan: Recap — Redwood will: 1) share micro-benchmark spreadsheet and perf logs, 2) provide warmup and pre-alloc scripts, 3) prepare NVLink multi-GPU trace example, 4) propose pilot schedule. Orchid will: 1) provide node inventory and driver matrix, 2) provide sample long-doc requests and traces, 3) allocate pilot nodes.
[00:12:33] Sanjay: That works. Anything else?
[00:12:36] Rina: Please include a short paragraph on security for cross-GPU memory and KMS flow.
[00:12:40] Jordan: We'll include that in the artifact share.
[00:12:42] Priya: Alright thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the sheet and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[00:12:48] Liam: Thanks, appreciate it.
[00:12:50] Jordan: Thanks all. End.

(End of recording)
